analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal land and offshore waters to oil and gas drilling while easing environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let states take over issuing federal oil and gas drilling permits on federal land, barred federal regulation of hydraulic fracturing in states with their own rules, and replaced the formal drilling permit with a simple notification that becomes final if the Interior Department does not object within 45 days. It would have expanded fast-track exemptions from environmental review for drilling, limited the President's power to keep offshore areas off-limits to drilling, and mandated new lease sales in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico. It also directed faster permitting for marine mammal harm from offshore activity and created leasing priority areas for geothermal, wind, and solar on public lands.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: faster permits, fewer environmental reviews, state-controlled permitting, expanded access to federal land and offshore waters, and new mandated lease sales in the Eastern Gulf. Coal operators gain limits on leasing moratoriums, and offshore energy firms gain easier marine mammal take authorizations. Coastal states named in the bill (Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Alaska) and Gulf producing states gain a share of offshore drilling revenue. Geothermal, wind, and solar developers gain designated leasing priority areas and streamlined geothermal exploration.

how_it_helps.text: Lets states with approved programs take over issuing federal Applications for Permit to Drill and approving drilling plans on federal land within their borders, and lets them collect the permitting fees instead of the federal government [S3].
Bars the Interior Department from enforcing any federal hydraulic fracturing rule in a state that has its own fracking regulations, deferring to state rules for fracking on federal land [S3].
Creates a notification-of-permit-to-drill process in developed fields: if the Secretary does not object within 45 days, the operator may drill and produce without any federal permit action [S3].

Makes a long list of oil and gas activities categorically excluded from National Environmental Policy Act review, with no requirement to check for extraordinary circumstances, and voids existing presidential withdrawals of Outer Continental Shelf areas from drilling except sanctuaries, monuments, and Bristol Bay [S3].

Establishes a revenue-sharing framework sending a growing share of Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas revenue to Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alaska, and increases Gulf producing states' share under the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act [S3].
Directs the Interior Department to offer all non-excluded Eastern Gulf of Mexico acreage for lease in multiple sales between 2021 and 2022 and each year after [S3].

Requires faster processing of marine mammal incidental-take authorizations, limits the conditions agencies can impose, deems authorizations granted if the agency misses deadlines, and exempts authorized takes from Endangered Species Act consultation [S3].

Directs the Interior Department to establish geothermal, solar, and wind leasing priority areas on federal land and gives categorical-exclusion treatment to small geothermal exploration test wells [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the environmental and fiscal costs: more drilling on public lands and offshore waters with reduced federal environmental review, weakened protections for marine mammals and endangered species, a reduced Treasury share of offshore revenue that would otherwise fund the general budget, and a $150-plus filing fee that raises the cost of protesting a lease sale. Future generations bear the climate and conservation cost of locking in expanded fossil fuel development.

drawbacks.text: Drilling from non-federal surface into federal minerals (where the government owns less than half the minerals) would be categorically excluded from analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Endangered Species Act [S3].
If the Interior Department misses the 45-day objection window on a notification of permit to drill, drilling and production can proceed with no federal approval action at all [S3].
The marine mammal provisions remove the 'least practicable impact' mitigation standard and deem an authorization issued on the applicant's own terms if the agency misses its 120-day deadline [S3].

The bill would bar the President from designating any new marine national monuments in ocean waters and would strip the President's general authority to withdraw Outer Continental Shelf areas from drilling, leaving that power only with Congress [S3].
Filing an administrative protest against a lease sale would cost a base fee of $150 plus $5 per page over ten pages, raising the cost for citizens and groups that challenge drilling leases [S3].

In the final revenue-sharing phase, 50 percent of Outer Continental Shelf revenue from new leases would flow to states instead of the Treasury, reducing federal revenue available to all taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has genuine features a supporter would cite: named coastal states get a share of offshore revenue, coastal towns and counties get dedicated funding for beaches, ports, and conservation, and the renewable energy title speeds geothermal, wind, and solar leasing. But the core of the bill is an expansion of oil and gas development with substantially weakened federal oversight — state takeover of federal permitting, a 45-day deemed-approved drilling notification, broad categorical exclusions from environmental review, and limits on presidential authority to protect offshore areas. The tradeoff heavily favors drilling operators, and the environmental review shortcuts shift risk onto public lands, coastal waters, and marine life.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to three of its subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Scalise introduced the American Energy First Act on September 11, 2019, joined by five original cosponsors [S3].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced, and four days later was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands, and the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the public kept the existing federal permitting, environmental review, and presidential offshore-protection authorities, and the oil and gas industry did not obtain the expanded access and streamlined permitting the bill would have granted. No state received the new offshore revenue sharing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept existing drilling safeguards

for.name: Rep. Steve Scalise
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Energy First Act and recruited five original cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote after it was referred to his committee

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, no vote was ever taken, and the bill died in the Democratic-controlled committee without action.

industries.note: The bill would give operators faster permits on federal land, state-run permitting, broad exemptions from environmental review, mandated Eastern Gulf lease sales, and new offshore access. The public bears the environmental and climate cost of that expansion.
Title IV limits the Interior Department's authority to impose leasing moratoriums on federal coal without an act of Congress, protecting coal leasing from future executive curbs.

industries.industry: Offshore seismic and drilling service firms
industries.note: The marine mammal provisions speed incidental-take authorizations, weaken mitigation requirements, and exempt authorized takes from Endangered Species Act consultation, lowering compliance costs for offshore surveys and drilling.

The bill designates renewable energy leasing priority areas on federal land and streamlines geothermal exploration, though its noncompetitive geothermal leasing provision lets adjacent land go to a single lessee without competition.

industries.industry: Coastal and Gulf producing state governments
industries.note: Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Alaska, and Gulf states would receive shares of offshore drilling revenue for coastal restoration, ports, and related uses — funds tied to expanded offshore drilling off their coasts.
